title: Maricha's last breath
hookLine: the deer leads Rama far from the hut, and its last breath carries a name
carry: remember God at the last breath

cards: Rama takes his bow, buckles on his sword, and goes. The deer lets him get close, then bounds away. It vanishes into the trees, then appears again in a clearing, glowing, waiting.
It runs, stops, looks back. Valmiki says it seemed to be playing with him: sometimes near, sometimes far, sometimes gone altogether.
And every time it reappears, it's a little farther from the hut, from Sita, and from Lakshmana.

teach.b: At last Rama is tired, angry, and very far from home. He fits an arrow, blazing like a snake, the text says, and shoots. The arrow strikes the deer in the heart, and as it falls, the disguise falls away.
On the ground lies Maricha, huge and bleeding, his real shape back. With his last breath he finishes Ravana's plan. He cries out in a perfect copy of Rama's voice: Ha Sita!
Ha Lakshmana! Then he dies. Rama, Valmiki says, is afraid.
If Sita hears that cry, what will she make Lakshmana do? He runs back toward the hut. Valmiki stops there.
But Hindu devotion has never let Maricha go so simply.
In Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, as Maricha gives up his life, he remembers Rama with love, and Rama grants him a place even sages find hard to reach. The villain, freed. Why?
Because of one of Hinduism's oldest beliefs about death: what the mind holds at the end matters.

teach.h: THE GITA: REMEMBER ME AT THE END.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says whoever leaves the body remembering him comes to him. So many Hindu families keep God's name close to the dying, with bhajans and the name said softly in the room.
In North India, mourners carry the body to the fire calling, Ram naam satya hai: Rama's name is truth. You can't cram for that moment.

teach.h: REMEMBER GOD AT THE LAST BREATH.
teach.b: You practice the name for a lifetime, so it's there at the last breath.

how: The deer's cry in Rama's voice is the turning point before Sita's abduction. At Hindu deathbeds many families sing bhajans and say God's name, and in North India mourners call out 'Ram naam satya hai' on the way to the cremation ground.

o: the deer who dies crying out in Rama's voice
the rakshasa who carries Sita off in a chariot
a rakshasa Lakshmana kills to guard the hut

s: Maricha cries out in Rama's voice as he dies
Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana!, to draw Lakshmana away.
in Valmiki, Maricha is freed by remembering Rama
that's devotional tellings like Tulsidas's; Valmiki just tells the death.
Hindus believe what the mind holds at the last breath matters
in the Gita, Krishna says whoever leaves the body remembering him comes to him.

games.q: Nani's old friend is near the end of her life, at home. her family plays bhajans and says Ram's name softly in her room. Sam asks why. what fits today's teaching?
o: so God's name is what her mind holds at the end, as the Gita teaches.
it just fills the quiet; any music would do.
the name is medicine, so it will cure her.
games.why: Hindus keep the name near the dying because the mind at the end matters. it's practiced for a lifetime so it's there then.

practice: Hindus practice the name every day so it's there when it matters most. Try it now. Softly say Shri Ram, Jai Ram, Jai Jai Ram, a chant many families sing, eleven times, slow, one breath each.
If you don't pray, choose one word that steadies you and repeat it the same way. When the mind wanders off, come back to the name.

wordCard.voice: Maricha. The deer's disguise falls away when Rama's arrow strikes, and he dies crying out in Rama's voice: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana!

orig.note: Hindi: Rama's name is truth. called out by mourners in North India as they carry the body to the cremation ground.

carryVoice: Carry this: remember God at the last breath. Back at the hut, Sita hears the cry. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 44 (the chase; Maricha's death; the cry)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kanda (Maricha remembers Rama as he dies and is given a state hard even for sages)
Bhagavad Gita 8.5 (whoever leaves the body remembering me comes to me)
